title: PHARAOH ORDERED HER TO KILL THE BABIES. SHE CHOSE TO FEAR GOD INSTEAD.
paragraphs: PHARAOH ORDERED HER TO KILL THE BABIES. SHE CHOSE TO FEAR GOD INSTEAD.
Her name was Shiphrah. She had no throne, no army, and no earthly power. But one decision in a delivery room exposed the limits of an empire—and revealed the kind of courage God never forgets.
There was a moment in ancient Egypt when a woman's hands were expected to become instruments of murder.
Those hands had spent years helping mothers bring children into the world. They had touched tiny fingers, wiped newborn faces, and witnessed the trembling relief of women who had survived childbirth.
But now the king wanted those same hands stained with innocent blood.
And the terrifying part?
The command came from the most powerful man in the nation.
Disobey him, and she could lose everything.
Obey him, and innocent children would die.
Her name was Shiphrah.
And before you dismiss her story as something that happened thousands of years ago, consider this:
What happens when doing what is right threatens everything you've worked to protect?
What happens when obedience to God could cost you your position, your security, your reputation, or even your life?
What happens when the world demands something your conscience knows is evil?
Because somewhere between Pharaoh's command and the cries of newborn children, Shiphrah faced a decision that still confronts believers today.
Will you fear the person who can threaten your future, or will you trust the God who holds eternity?
And there is something extraordinary buried in this account.
Scripture remembers the name of the woman who refused to obey Pharaoh.
But the Pharaoh who gave the command?
In this passage, he remains unnamed.
Don't miss what that means.
The ruler had the throne.
The midwife had a name.
And thousands of years later, we are still speaking hers.
Exodus 1 opens with a nation growing under oppression.

The descendants of Israel had multiplied in Egypt. What began with the family of Jacob had become a numerous people. But a new king arose who did not know Joseph, and instead of seeing Israel's growth as something to be respected, he saw it as a threat.
Fear became policy.
Policy became oppression.
Oppression became brutality.
The Egyptians forced the Israelites into hard labor, but the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied.
Then Pharaoh escalated his cruelty.
He summoned two Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, and commanded them to kill the male Hebrew babies during childbirth while allowing the girls to live.
The Hebrew text of Exodus 1:16 contains the chilling instruction:
אִם־בֵּן הוּא וַהֲמִתֶּן אֹתוֹ
Im-ben hu, vahamitten oto.
A close translation is:
“If it is a son, you shall put him to death.”
No ambiguity.
No misunderstanding.
This was not ordinary government administration. It was an order to murder defenseless children because of their identity.
Imagine being summoned before the king and hearing those words.
Imagine returning to your work knowing that every birth could now become a test of your loyalty.
Imagine a mother looking into your eyes, trusting you with the most vulnerable moment of her life.
And knowing that the government had ordered you to betray that trust.
The Bible does not describe Shiphrah's private thoughts. It does not tell us whether her hands trembled, whether she struggled to sleep, or whether she feared punishment.
We must not invent those details as history.
But we know the decision she and Puah made.
And the words of Scripture are astonishing.
“But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.” — Exodus 1:17, KJV
Read that again.
They feared God.
And they let the boys live.
Not because Pharaoh had become merciful.
Not because the law had changed.
Not because obedience was convenient.
They refused because a higher moral authority stood above the throne of Egypt.
The Hebrew expression is:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
Vattirena hamyalledot et-ha'Elohim.
“The midwives feared God.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root יָרֵא (yare), associated with fear, reverence, and awe.
In this context, fearing God was not merely an inward religious feeling.
It became an outward act of costly obedience.
They recognized that Pharaoh's authority was not ultimate.
God's authority was.
And that changes how we understand courage.
Courage is not always the absence of fear.
Sometimes courage is knowing exactly what obedience might cost—and refusing to surrender your conscience anyway.
Some of you reading this know what that feels like.
Maybe nobody has ordered you to commit the evil Pharaoh commanded. Your circumstances may be entirely different.
But you know what it means to face pressure.
The pressure to falsify something at work because everyone else does it.
The pressure to remain silent when someone vulnerable is being mistreated.
The pressure to compromise your convictions to keep a relationship.
The pressure to pretend that something sinful is acceptable because telling the truth might make you unpopular.
And sometimes the hardest battle is not against a cruel ruler.
Sometimes it is against the desperate voice inside you whispering:
Just do what they want. You cannot afford to lose anything else.
Shiphrah's story confronts that voice.
Not with a promise that obedience will always be safe.
But with the truth that God is worthy of obedience even when obedience is costly.
Yet there is another woman we must not overlook.
Puah.
Her name appears beside Shiphrah's because Scripture presents their courage together.
They were not competing for recognition.
They stood against the same evil.
They protected the same vulnerable lives.
And their names were preserved together.
There is something beautiful about that.
Sometimes God strengthens your faith through someone who refuses to let you stand alone.
A friend who tells you the truth when everyone else flatters you.
A brother or sister in Christ who prays with you when compromise seems easier.
A believer who quietly says, “We cannot do that. We belong to Jesus.”
Not every act of faithfulness happens on a platform.
Not every courageous believer becomes famous.
Sometimes the kingdom of God is served through two people who agree that they will not participate in evil.
And heaven does not need an audience to recognize faithfulness.
But the story becomes even more intense.
Pharaoh discovers that the male children are still living.
He summons the midwives again.
“Why have ye done this thing, and have saved the men children alive?” — Exodus 1:18, KJV
Imagine the weight of that question.
The king knew his command had not been carried out.
The women now stood accountable before the very authority they had disobeyed.
Their response, recorded in Exodus 1:19, was that the Hebrew women were vigorous and gave birth before the midwives arrived.
This part of the story deserves careful handling.

The passage does not provide enough information for us to determine every circumstance behind their explanation. Christians have differed over whether it was entirely factual, strategically incomplete, or deceptive.
We should not use the account to make dishonesty a virtue.
What the text explicitly commends is their fear of God and their refusal to kill the children.
And what happens next is remarkable.
“Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty.” — Exodus 1:20, KJV
God dealt well with them.
The Hebrew reads:
וַיֵּיטֶב אֱלֹהִים לַמְיַלְּדֹת
Vayyetav Elohim lamyalledot.
A close rendering is:
“And God did good to the midwives.”
Then Exodus 1:21 explains:
“And it came to pass, because the midwives feared God, that he made them houses.” — KJV
The Hebrew expression וַיַּעַשׂ לָהֶם בָּתִּים (vayya'as lahem batim) literally speaks of making “houses” for them.
In this context, many interpreters understand it to refer to God establishing households or families for the midwives, rather than simply constructing physical buildings.
Scripture does not tell us all the details of that blessing.
But it does tell us why God dealt favorably with them.
They feared Him.
Now be careful here.
This is not a formula promising that every courageous Christian will receive financial prosperity, a comfortable home, or protection from suffering.
The Bible itself shows faithful people who endure imprisonment, rejection, persecution, and death.
Hebrews 11 celebrates believers who experienced extraordinary deliverance alongside others who suffered terribly while remaining faithful.
Shiphrah's story is not proof that obedience purchases an easy life.
It is evidence that God sees faithfulness that earthly powers overlook.
And perhaps that is what someone needs to hear today.
You have been trying to do the right thing, but nobody seems to notice.
You refused a dishonest opportunity, and someone else got ahead.
You walked away from a sinful relationship, and now the loneliness hurts.
You chose forgiveness when bitterness felt justified.
You told the truth, and it cost you something.
You prayed.
You obeyed.
You tried to remain faithful.
And somewhere along the way, you began wondering whether God had forgotten.
But Shiphrah's name still stands in Scripture.
Not because she controlled the outcome.
Not because she possessed worldly greatness.
But because she feared God when a powerful man demanded evil.
The world may never applaud your obedience. That does not mean God has overlooked it.
And now comes a detail that makes the story even more significant.
Pharaoh's command failed.
The boys continued to live.
The people continued to multiply.
And the ruler who attempted to suppress Israel could not stop God's purposes.
But Pharaoh did not surrender.
Exodus 1:22 records that he escalated the violence, commanding his people to cast every Hebrew son into the Nile.
The threat became even more widespread.
This is important because it prevents us from romanticizing the story.
Shiphrah and Puah's courage did not instantly end oppression.
Their obedience was real.
God's favor was real.
And the suffering of Israel was still real.
Sometimes faithfulness changes a life without immediately changing an entire system.
Sometimes a righteous decision saves someone today while the wider battle continues tomorrow.
That does not make the decision meaningless.
It makes it necessary.
And then, in the very next chapter, a child is born.
A Hebrew boy.
His mother hides him for three months.
When she can no longer conceal him, she places him in a basket among the reeds by the river.
That child is Moses.
Scripture does not say Shiphrah or Puah personally delivered Moses or saved him. We must not claim that they did.
But their story belongs to the same unfolding account of God's preservation of His people.
Pharaoh tried to destroy Israel's sons.
Yet God would raise up a son of Israel to confront Pharaoh.
The king who commanded babies to be thrown into the river would eventually face a man who had been rescued from that very river.
What a reversal.
And still, Moses was not the ultimate Savior.
He was a servant through whom God delivered Israel from Egyptian bondage.
The greater deliverance would come through Jesus Christ.
And this is where Shiphrah's story becomes more than an inspiring account of human courage.
It leads us toward the heart of the Gospel.
Because centuries later, another ruler would feel threatened by the birth of a child.
Matthew 2 records that Herod, seeking to destroy the young Jesus, ordered the killing of boys in Bethlehem and its surrounding region who were two years old and under.
Once again, a ruler responded to perceived danger with violence against children.
Once again, the innocent were threatened by the powerful.
And once again, the purposes of God were not defeated.
Joseph was warned in a dream and took Mary and Jesus to Egypt.
Think about that.
The land once associated with Pharaoh's oppression became a place of refuge for the child who would save His people from their sins.
Matthew presents Jesus' return from Egypt in connection with Hosea 11:1:
“Out of Egypt have I called my son.” — Matthew 2:15, KJV
The biblical story is not a collection of disconnected moral lessons.
It is the unfolding revelation of God's redemptive purposes, culminating in Christ.
And Jesus came to accomplish something no human midwife, prophet, or deliverer could accomplish.
He came to rescue sinners from the judgment and bondage of sin.
Shiphrah refused to become an instrument of death.
Jesus willingly entered a world ruled by sin and death so that, through His own death and resurrection, He could bring eternal life to those who believe.
Shiphrah's obedience preserved vulnerable lives.
Christ's perfect obedience secured salvation for His people.
Romans 5:19 teaches that through the obedience of the One, many will be made righteous.
And Philippians 2:8 declares that Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
There is our hope.
Not that we can become brave enough to earn God's acceptance.
Not that our good deeds can erase our guilt.
Not that our sacrifices can purchase salvation.
Our hope is Jesus Christ, who obeyed perfectly where we have failed and gave Himself for sinners who could never save themselves.
And perhaps this is the moment the story stops being about Shiphrah.
And starts being about you.
Because you may admire her courage while secretly remembering the moments when you did not have it.
The moment you knew the truth but remained silent.
The moment you chose approval over obedience.
The moment you compromised because you were afraid of losing someone.
The moment you followed the crowd even though your conscience was troubled.
Maybe you have carried the memory for years.
Maybe you have convinced everyone around you that you are spiritually strong.
You know the worship songs.
You know the right words.
You know how to smile at church.
But there are decisions in your past that still haunt you.
And the question you are afraid to ask is not, “Could I have been like Shiphrah?”
It is:
“Can God still receive someone who has failed to be faithful?”
Listen carefully.
Yes.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because grace gives us permission to continue in rebellion.
But because Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Peter denied knowing Jesus three times.
And after the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The thief on the cross had no opportunity to rebuild his reputation or perform a lifetime of religious works.
Yet when he turned to Jesus in faith, Christ promised him paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
And the apostle Paul, who had persecuted the church, later testified that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).
Do you see it?
The Gospel is not merely an invitation to admire brave people.
It is an invitation to come to the Savior who forgives cowards, restores the fallen, cleanses the guilty, and transforms those who surrender to Him.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
That does not mean He erases the historical consequences of every choice.
It means your sin does not have to be the final word over your life.
The cross declares that sin is serious enough to require the death of the Son of God.
The resurrection declares that death itself could not hold Him.
And the Gospel calls you to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Maybe your next act of courage is not confronting a Pharaoh.
Maybe it is confessing a sin you have hidden.
Maybe it is apologizing to someone you wounded.
Maybe it is refusing to participate in wrongdoing even if it costs you.
Maybe it is protecting someone who has no power to protect themselves.
Maybe it is finally admitting that your religious appearance has been hiding a heart that desperately needs Christ.
Whatever it is, do not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation.
The Holy Spirit does not expose sin merely to leave repentant sinners drowning in shame.
He points us to Christ, in whom forgiveness and new life are found.
First John 1:9 reminds us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
That is not permission to live carelessly.
It is freedom to stop hiding.
Freedom to repent.
Freedom to begin walking in obedience—not to purchase salvation, but because grace has brought you to the Savior.
Shiphrah feared God more than Pharaoh.
And perhaps today you need to ask yourself:
Whose approval has become more important to me than the Lord's?
What have I been calling “necessary” that Scripture calls sin?
What truth have I been avoiding because obedience might change my life?
And where is Jesus calling me to trust Him rather than surrender to fear?
Do not rush past those questions.
Some of the most important spiritual battles happen when nobody else is watching.
There may be no audience.
No applause.
No public recognition.
Only a decision between what is convenient and what is right.
But that decision matters.
You can simply write “I'm still fighting.”
Not as a declaration that your strength is enough.
But as a confession that you still need the grace of Jesus Christ and the prayers of His people.

And if Christ has already brought you through a season when you thought your faith would collapse, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading may need to know that repentance, restoration, and renewed obedience are possible through Him.
There is no shame in asking your brothers and sisters to pray.
There is no spiritual prize for pretending you never struggle.
And there is no substitute for bringing your heart honestly before God.
Shiphrah's courage was not the source of Israel's salvation.
God was.
And your courage will never be the source of your salvation either.
Jesus is.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
Not to replace the local church, pastoral care, or the fellowship of believers.
But to keep pointing people back to the Scriptures, back to repentance, back to the cross, and back to the risen Savior.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who have not opened a Bible in months.
People who feel disqualified by their past.
People quietly wrestling with unbelief.
People who know how to appear happy while their homes are falling apart.
People who need more than another inspirational quote.
They need the truth of Jesus Christ.
That is why I want to ask something personal.
Not merely because you enjoyed reading it.
But because someone among your friends may be facing a decision that requires courage, or carrying guilt that only the Gospel can address.
It is not a replacement for repentance, faith, or obedience.
And it should never be treated as a requirement for glorifying God.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, including how we steward the resources He entrusts to us.
It is distinct from giving to your local church and should not be presented as a required biblical tithe.
But it can be a sincere expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
It is the opportunity to help biblical truth reach another person.
Another struggling believer.
Another discouraged parent.
Another young person questioning whether following Jesus is worth the cost.
Another wounded soul who needs to hear that forgiveness is found in Christ.
Read the Word.
Pray.
Serve faithfully in your church.
Love your neighbor.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone.
Every act of obedience offered to God matters, whether or not money is involved.
The goal is to make much of Jesus.
And now, before you leave, I want you to picture the story one final time.
An Egyptian throne.
A royal command.
Two Hebrew midwives.
And newborn children who could not defend themselves.
Pharaoh possessed the machinery of an empire.
Shiphrah and Puah possessed no comparable political power.
Yet the king could command them to do evil, and they could refuse.
They could not control everything that happened next.
They could not guarantee their own safety.
They could not end all the suffering of their people.
But they could fear God.
And they did.
Centuries passed.
The empire changed.
Its rulers died.
Its monuments weathered.
But the names Shiphrah and Puah remained in the Word of God.
And now their testimony has reached you.
Not so you can admire them for a moment and return unchanged to whatever compromise has been ruling your heart.
But so you can remember that obedience matters, even when it is unseen.
That innocent lives matter.
That human authority is never greater than God's moral law.
That faithfulness may be costly.
And that the Savior who calls you to follow Him is also the Savior whose grace is sufficient for repentant sinners who have failed.
So when fear whispers, “You cannot afford to obey,” remember Shiphrah.
When shame whispers, “You have failed too badly to return,” remember Peter—and the risen Christ who restored him.
And when the world whispers, “Your life is too small to matter,” remember the two women whose names outlived the king who threatened them.
But above all, remember Jesus.
The One who was obedient unto death.
The One who bore our sins on the cross.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through faith in Him.
The One who does not merely inspire better behavior, but gives new life.
So be honest before God today.
What is the one thing you need to surrender to Jesus?
Let it be more than words on a screen.
Let it become a prayer you carry into your next difficult decision.
Because in the end, the greatest miracle of this story is not that a king's command was resisted.
It is that the God who saw two faithful women in Egypt is the same God who has made Himself known to us through Jesus Christ.
And in Him, there is forgiveness for your yesterday, grace for your today, and hope for your tomorrow.
Pharaoh had the power to threaten their lives—but he never had the power to make God forget their names.
